description: Looking down at our planet, we see a changing world—and a world of possibilities. Our team is on a journey to connect ecosystems and listen to what the Earth is whispering through space data. By finding where today's landscapes mirror tomorrow's horizons, we are planting the seeds for a greener, more adaptable future. 🌿✨
summary: Future Twin uses satellite data and climate modeling to match our farm with an existing successful "twin," bypassing risky trial-and-error to guarantee sustainable crop yields.
details:
1. What does it do or how does it work?

Project Concept:

Future Twin is a smart agriculture project that integrates soil analysis, future climate projections, and global geographic analog discovery to help farms anticipate climate change impacts and make informed agricultural decisions.

How It Works:

  1. Global Search and Filtering: Searches across global datasets to identify locations with climatic and soil conditions similar to those expected at the target farm in the future. The target site, "My Farm" (Savola), covers 900 feddans and is located in Egypt at 27.76° N, 30.33° E.
  2. Climate and Soil Analog Modeling: Analyzes future climate projections from NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 under SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios, alongside SoilGrids data (0–30 cm), including soil texture, pH, soil organic carbon (SOC), and cation exchange capacity (CEC).
  3. Satellite Remote Sensing Analysis (2015–2026): Uses Google Earth Engine to analyze 12 years of satellite data through vegetation and environmental indicators, including NDVI (vegetation health), NDWI (moisture conditions), and salinity indices.
  4. Optimal Future Twin Selection: Ranks candidate locations and identifies the most suitable reference site. Farm A achieved 94.6% overall climatic similarity. Its historical agricultural conditions and management practices provide a reference for developing adaptation strategies, including adjusting wheat and sugar beet planting windows to November 16 onward.
2. What benefits does it have?
  • Climate Resilience: Helps farms prepare for rising temperatures, increasing heat stress days (>35°C), and higher evapotranspiration (ET₀) demands.
  • Water Resource Optimization: Supports more efficient irrigation planning by learning from agricultural management practices in locations already experiencing similar environmental conditions.
  • Risk Reduction: Reduces dependence on costly trial-and-error approaches by using historical observations, soil information, and future climate projections to guide agricultural decisions.
  • Better Agricultural Planning: Provides farmers and agronomists with location-specific insights to support crop management and adaptation strategies.
3. What is the intended impact of the project?
  • Sustainable Food Security: Supports the long-term productivity of strategic crops, particularly wheat and sugar beet, under changing climatic conditions.
  • Data-Driven Decision Making: Empowers farmers, agronomists, and agricultural decision-makers in Egypt and other arid regions to move from reactive farming practices toward predictive, science-based planning.
  • Climate Adaptation: Provides a practical framework for identifying agricultural regions that can serve as real-world references for future farming conditions.
  • Scalability: Establishes a methodology that can be applied to different farms, crops, and geographic regions worldwide.
4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

AI and Collaborative Development Tools:

  • Manus
  • Google Gemini
  • Claude
  • ChatGPT (GPT)
  • OpenCode

Geospatial and Cloud Computing Platforms:

  • Google Earth Engine (GEE) and Earth Engine Code Editor.
  • Google Colab (Python).
  • ArcGIS Pro (Esri).

Datasets and Scientific Data Sources:

  • NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6: Future climate projections under SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios.
  • NASA LP DAAC – GFSAD 1 km Crop Mask 2010: Agricultural land identification and cropland masking.
  • NASA SRTM: Digital elevation data accessed through Google Earth Engine (USGS/SRTMGL1_003).
  • ERA5-Land (ECMWF/Copernicus C3S): Historical climate and environmental variables.
  • SoilGrids (ISRIC – World Soil Information): Global soil physical and chemical property datasets.
5. How is your project creative?

Dynamic Time-Space Connection:

Unlike conventional agricultural monitoring systems that primarily analyze historical conditions, Future Twin connects future climate projections with existing real-world locations that already experience similar environmental conditions. It identifies a present-day geographic reference for a farm's projected future environment.

Integration of Multiple Scientific Disciplines:

The project combines three major scientific components into one integrated workflow:

  • Future climate analog modeling using NASA climate projections.
  • Physical and chemical soil analysis to evaluate soil compatibility.
  • Long-term satellite remote sensing analysis using vegetation, moisture, and salinity indicators from 2015 to 2026.

Learning from Real-World Agricultural Experience:

Rather than relying exclusively on theoretical predictions, Future Twin uses the historical environmental and agricultural conditions of selected analog locations to help identify potential challenges and adaptation opportunities for the target farm.

6. What factors did your team consider?

Climate Indicators:

  • Maximum monthly temperatures.
  • Growing Degree Days (GDD).
  • Seasonal reference evapotranspiration (ET₀).
  • Frost days.
  • Heat stress days (temperatures above 35°C).

Soil Compatibility:

The analysis considers soil texture compatibility, particularly Sandy Clay Loam, alongside important physical and chemical properties:

  • Soil pH.
  • Electrical Conductivity (EC).
  • Soil Organic Carbon (SOC).
  • Cation Exchange Capacity (CEC).
  • Calcium Carbonate (CaCO₃).
